public_rationale: Several AI startups did cut back in the months after June 2025. Cursor moved Pro from 500 requests to $20 of included usage on June 16. Augment Code said its pricing was unsustainable and moved to credits in October, raising costs for heavy users. The Register reported Augment's CEO citing similar changes at Zed, Replit, and Cursor. These fit the austerity he describes. But his claim is about 'just about every AI startup', and that they 'had to'. I found no representative evidence on how many AI startups changed pricing or limits in that window, and the examples are mostly coding tools. A handful of instances cannot confirm a near-universal claim, and I found no counterexamples to refute it. So it stays unresolved.
limitations: Prevalence across all AI startups is not measured anywhere I found.
Replit's change is shown only through a news mention, not its primary post.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: After the June 2025 priority tiers, nearly every AI startup had to institute austerity.

statement.excerpt: Over the next few months, just about every AI startup had to institute some form of austerity.
statement.document_title: The Subprime AI Crisis Is Here

from_speaker: had to institute some form of austerity
after OpenAI and Anthropic priority tiers starting June 2025
our_interpretation: 'Austerity' means price increases, tighter usage limits, a switch from flat or request-based plans to usage or credit pricing that raises costs for heavy users, or feature cuts made to control costs.
'Just about every AI startup' means a large majority of AI startups that resell frontier-model access, especially coding and app-builder tools. It does not mean only the handful he names.
'Had to' means the changes were driven by cost pressure, not optional product choices.
Period: 'the next few months' after June 2025, read as June through December 2025.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that most AI startups reselling model access (not just a few named ones) raised prices, cut limits, or moved to cost-reflective pricing between June and December 2025 because of cost pressure.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that many comparable AI startups kept pricing and limits unchanged or made them more generous in that window, or that changes were few or not cost-driven.

evidence.excerpt: We moved from request-based pricing to $20 of included usage on Pro.
evidence.locator: section 'Why did we change the plan?'
evidence.explanation: Cursor limited included frontier-model use on its Pro plan in June 2025. This is one instance of the austerity he describes. It does not show prevalence.

evidence.excerpt: The user message model also isn’t sustainable for Augment Code as a business.
evidence.explanation: Augment moved to credit pricing because of costs, which fits 'had to'. It is one more instance, not proof that most startups did the same.

evidence.excerpt: McClernan argued that usage-based pricing is "fast becoming the industry standard," referencing pricing changes from competitors including Zed, Replit, Cursor, and Anthropic.
evidence.explanation: A trend report naming several coding-tool startups that changed pricing. It suggests a broad shift in coding tools, but it is one CEO's description, not a survey of all AI startups.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A systematic dataset or survey of pricing and usage-limit changes at a broad set of AI startups from June to December 2025, ideally with stated reasons.
